description: Mater Amabilis Year 8 living books curriculum for grade 8. Demanding literature, layered historical analysis, and mature written narration as the Rhetoric stage begins.

books.title: The New World (A History of the English-Speaking Peoples, Vol. 2)
books.author: Winston Churchill
books.subject: history
books.notes: Dense, opinionated, adult prose — exactly the challenge this stage calls for. Push for written narration in the student's own analytical voice, not a summary. 'Do you agree with Churchill's judgment of this event, or would you argue differently?'

books.title: Plutarch's Lives (selected passages, continuing rotation)
books.author: Plutarch
books.subject: history
books.notes: The final years of the multi-year Plutarch rotation. Expect the student to weigh competing virtues against each other, not just narrate events. 'Which of this man's qualities would you keep, and which would you reject?'

books.title: Unknown to History: A Story of the Captivity of Mary of Scotland
books.author: Charlotte M. Yonge
books.subject: history
books.notes: Historical fiction that takes real captivity and real politics seriously. 'What does this story suggest about the cost of political loyalty?'

books.title: Emma
books.author: Jane Austen
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: Austen's most subtly ironic heroine — someone who means well and is repeatedly wrong. 'Where does Emma deceive herself, and how does she find that out?'

books.title: The Pickwick Papers (selections)
books.author: Charles Dickens
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: Dickens at his most purely comic — good contrast against the heavier history reading this term. 'What is Dickens making fun of here, and is it kind or cruel humor?'

books.title: The Innocence of Father Brown (selected stories)
books.author: G. K. Chesterton
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: A quiet priest who solves crimes through moral insight rather than forensic cleverness. 'What did Father Brown understand about the criminal that the detectives missed?'

books.title: The Merchant of Venice
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: The full play, after the Lamb retelling met years earlier. Read some scenes aloud, in parts. 'Is Portia's famous mercy speech actually merciful in how the trial ends?'

books.title: Everyman (medieval morality play)
books.author: Anonymous
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: A short, strange, entirely allegorical play — every character is a virtue or vice with a name to match. 'Which of Everyman's companions actually goes with him in the end, and why?'

subject_plans.art_music: Composer: Ludwig van Beethoven — emotionally complex, biographically compelling (composing through encroaching deafness). Good subject for discussing how adversity shaped an artist's work, fitting the Rhetoric stage's capacity for nuance. Artist: Michelangelo — Renaissance mastery across sculpture, painting, and architecture (David, the Sistine Chapel ceiling); rich material for discussing technical skill alongside spiritual and human themes. Poet: William Wordsworth — philosophical Romantic poetry on nature, memory, and the sublime; pairs naturally with this age's capacity for abstraction and this curriculum's nature-study emphasis.
subject_plans.greek: Year 8 scope (grade 8) — Greek as a lens. The student reads familiar New Testament verses with confidence, traces a chain of English words back to one Greek root, and can say what the six terms mean together rather than one at a time. For a student who also takes Latin, this is the year the two subjects meet: put Matthew 22:37 and 39 side by side in both languages and let them see that caritas is translating agape and that the same sentence carries in both. Close by having the student say the Great Commandment in Greek from memory and explain why every other word in the subject hangs on it. Everything in this year is the shared inheritance of all Christian traditions — the Greek New Testament, the theological virtues, and the ordinary vocabulary of the faith — so a Protestant, Catholic, or Orthodox family can teach it in full. Introduce nothing specific to one tradition here (devotion to the saints or to Mary, the sacraments, prayers for the dead, icons, a particular church's authority or structure), and take no position on which Greek manuscript tradition is correct: every text supplied reads the same in both. Send any doctrinal question that divides Christian traditions to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister. All Greek quoted must come from the verbatim block supplied in the session — never recited from memory, never composed — and always shown with its transliteration and English.
subject_plans.language_arts: Grade 8: advanced grammar and composition, essay-length written narration expected as the default (not the exception), literary analysis vocabulary (theme, motif, irony, characterization), and early persuasive/rhetorical writing — the student should begin defending a position with evidence, not just summarizing a text.
subject_plans.latin: Year 8 scope (grade 8) — Latin as a lens. The student can read familiar Vulgate verses with confidence, trace a chain of English words back to one Latin root, and articulate what the six foundational terms mean together rather than one at a time: faith, hope, and love as how the Great Commandment is obeyed; wisdom and truth as what it takes to obey it well; prayer and work as the two halves of the day in which it is actually done. Close the year by having the student say the whole Great Commandment in Latin from memory and then explain, in their own words, why every other term in the subject hangs on it. Everything in this year is the shared inheritance of all Christian traditions — the Vulgate, the theological virtues, and the ordinary vocabulary of the faith — so a family of any Christian tradition can teach it in full. Introduce nothing specific to one tradition here (devotion to the saints or to Mary, the sacraments, prayers for the dead, a particular church's authority or structure); a family that wants that has Saints & Catechism as its own subject. Send any doctrinal question that divides Christian traditions to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister. All Latin quoted must come from the verbatim block supplied in the session — never recited from memory, never composed.
subject_plans.logic: Year 8 scope (grade 8) — reasoning as a habit. The remaining fallacies (hasty generalization, appeal to popularity, equivocation) and the ability to lay out an argument's premises and conclusion on paper where the structure becomes visible. The year's real work is the disposition rather than the content: turning the tools on one's own reasoning first, stating an opponent's case fairly, and understanding that naming a fallacy in someone's argument does not show their conclusion is false. Close the year on that last point — it is the difference between a thinker and a debater. Logic serves truth and charity, never winning an argument: teach the student to test their own reasoning first and to state the strongest version of the other side fairly before criticizing it. Never coach a child in arguing against their own parents' instructions or authority — a disagreement at home belongs to the family, not to a logic lesson. Take no position on contested political, moral, or religious disputes however logically the question is framed; teach the form with neutral examples and send the substance to the student's own parents, pastor, priest, or minister. Work only from the arguments supplied in the session — never invent a syllogism or a fallacy example, since an invalid argument can look perfectly sound and the student cannot yet catch that.
subject_plans.mathematics: Grade 8 scope (Common Core domains 8.NS, 8.EE, 8.F, 8.G, 8.SP): the real number system including irrational numbers; linear equations and systems of equations; an introduction to functions; geometric transformations and the Pythagorean theorem; scatter plots and bivariate data. Mater Amabilis approach at this stage (Rhetoric): the student should be able to justify each step of an argument, not just execute it — push for 'prove it' and 'is there another way to see this?'
subject_plans.morning_time: Scripture with real theological discussion, not just the passage's plain narrative; hymn and folksong from the term's rotation; Wordsworth for poetry, ideally followed by the student's own brief written or spoken response rather than passive listening only.
subject_plans.nature_study: Year 8 scope — the naturalist's own long study: a season-long observation of one chosen subject (a tree, a pond margin, a bird species, a patch of sky) recorded in the nature notebook with dated entries; identification using keys rather than being told; weather records kept and compared; the night sky by season; local geology and how the land got its shape; the ethics of observation — leaving a place as it was found. Charlotte Mason approach: at this age the notebook is the curriculum. Ask for the entry, then ask what changed since the last one and what the child expects next.
subject_plans.saints: Year 8 scope — holiness in hard circumstances, and the Church in the modern world: Thomas More and conscience; Edmund Campion; Kateri Tekakwitha; Elizabeth Ann Seton; Damien of Molokai; Thérèse of Lisieux and the little way; Maximilian Kolbe; Teresa of Calcutta. Virtue focus: fortitude and justice, and the examined conscience. Charlotte Mason approach: ask what the saint actually chose and what it cost, before naming the virtue. Bede informs conscience; it never replaces the child's own, and questions of a family's practice belong to their own priest.
subject_plans.science: Year 8 scope — physical science with real quantities: matter and the particle model; elements, compounds, and the periodic table's organisation; chemical change versus physical change; forces, motion, and Newton's three laws; energy transfer and conservation; waves, light, and sound; simple electricity and magnetism. Charlotte Mason approach: require a stated hypothesis and an honest account of what actually happened, including when it contradicted the expectation. A failed prediction, well described, is a better narration than a tidy one.
subject_plans.scripture: Year 8 scope — the whole canon in view: the Bible as one library and one story; how the Law, Prophets, and Writings relate to the Gospels and letters; major covenants traced end to end; Revelation read as hope under pressure rather than as a puzzle. Themes: justice, mercy, faithfulness, the moral law as the text plainly teaches it. Charlotte Mason approach: the child should be able to place any passage in the larger story and defend the placement. Expect disagreement to be argued from the text. Canon and translation are the family's own: follow whatever Bible they are reading and never assert that one tradition's canon, chapter ordering, or translation is the correct one. Teach the narrative and the moral law the text plainly states; leave denomination-specific doctrine — sacramental theology, church governance, a particular catechism's structure — to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister.
